I forgive your transgression. In the Vinaya, the correct term is *chān-hui* (懺悔). "Chān" (*chān*) means pure dharmas (*śukla-dharma*); "hui" (*hui*) means dark dharmas (*kṛṣṇa-dharma*).

This means that dark dharmas must be repented and not committed again, while pure dharmas must be aspired to and honored. Because the act of rejecting and the act of accepting are discussed together, it is called *chān-hui*.
Furthermore, "chān" means cultivating what comes; "hui" means reforming what has passed. This refers to the unwholesome deeds performed in the past.
Regarding the Dharma, one despises and loathes it, vowing never to commit it again; thus, it is called *hui* (repentance).

Regarding all wholesome dharmas discarded in the past, from this day forward, one vows to cultivate them diligently; thus, it is called *chan* (confession). Because one abandons what was past and seeks what is to come, it is called *chanhui* (repentance and confession).
Furthermore, *chan* means to lay bare all faults and expose one’s transgressions, not daring to conceal or hide them; this is *hui*.

It is called "severing the continuity of the mind. Through weariness, regret, and relinquishment, one is able to abandon both that which is done and that which is to be done; hence, it is termed "repentance" (*chān-hui*).
Furthermore, it is translated as "washing and dyeing to achieve purity," which illustrates the Dharma through a metaphor. The *Mahāsannipāta Sūtra* states:

For example, if a garment that has been soiled for a hundred years can be thoroughly washed and cleansed with diligent effort on a single day, it will immediately become bright and pure through human labor.

Repentance is likewise. Even if one has accumulated various unwholesome karmas throughout a hundred kalpas, if one can wash the mind and disclose them on a single day, repenting with earnest sincerity, then by means of the Buddha-dharma—
By the power of this, all transgressions are immediately extinguished; therefore, it is called "washing and dyeing to achieve purity.

Furthermore, *chan* (懺) means shame (*hrī*), and *hui* (悔) means remorse (*apatrāpya*). Shame refers to feeling ashamed before the heavens, while remorse refers to feeling ashamed before others. Others perceive its outward manifestation.

The heavens behold their obscurity. Obscurity is subtle while manifestation is coarse; both the coarse and the subtle are evil. Therefore, one should give rise to profound shame and remorse, and perform sincere repentance.

(After the assembly has prostrated three times before the Buddha, two people leading the *yin-ghing* bell lead the assembly out through the side doors and proceed toward Wei...)

The attendants stand in formation before the Vaiśravaṇa Hall. Those holding official duties follow behind, arranged from junior to senior. The two lead *qing* (hand-bells) remain in front of the incense burner.
They lead the Abbot to the entrance of the Vaiśravaṇa Hall. The attendant carries the incense burner forward through the middle gate and places it upon the offering table, standing by its side.
The *vinaya-dhara* (Venerable Leader) intones: (Chanting follows).
Vaiśravaṇa Deva General (etcetera). Mahāprajñāpāramitā of the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Samantacakṣu. (The assembly chants together.
The Abbot approaches the incense burner to inquire after [the Buddha’s] well-being. He takes up the incense and offers it three times. He inquires after [the Buddha’s] well-being again and again.
Upon the completion of the eulogy, the Abbot stands to the side. The assembly forms ranks facing upward. They perform three inquiries with utmost sincerity.)

The Abbot says: “I extend my most sincere greetings and look up to you for your protection and blessings, so that as we practice the Way during these ninety days, all demonic obstacles may be silently dispelled.
(After the greetings, the leader of the group closes the door and says: “We prostrate three times to the Abbot” (or say: “We go to the Abbot’s quarters to prostrate to the Abbot.
(The Abbot may say: “Exempt from bowing” (or say: “One bow. This is what is meant by relying on a Vinaya Master to seek his guidance in all matters.

[After bowing: "The methods for applying the mind while practicing the Way during the time of activity and conduct. The Abbot says: "Each person shall come in order to enter the summer retreat (*an-gyo*).

The leaders remain outside; everyone must look after one another. [The Abbot proceeds to the *fang-wang* (abbot’s quarters), followed by either the Head Seat Master (*shōza-shi*) or the *karma*-master.]
The Three Methods for *Varṣā* (Rainy Season Retreat) Performed Before a Counterpart (divided into two parts). First, regarding the reliance on the place rather than the person:
"reliance on the place rather than the person" refers to the presiding master of the Dharma and the senior monks (*sthavira*) who are learned in the Vinaya.

Generally speaking, those who preside over the administration of the Vinaya serve as the support for the community; their status belongs to the lineage of teachers and is not comparable to that of ordinary members of the assembly.
The Elder is the leader among the assembly and a venerable master who knows the Dharma; although he does not preside over the Dharma, he is not merely one who relies on his own learning.
For this reason, the questions and answers regarding the *varṣā* (rainy season retreat) differ slightly from the norm, in that one should rely solely upon the location and not upon the person.
If the ritual procedures were not set out separately, there would be no fixed standard to rely upon at the time of the ceremony. Should one consider oneself to be...

Venerable Sir, if one does not address another person with a formal declaration (*pratideśanā*), it cannot be called "entering the summer retreat" (*varṣopagamana*). How, then, can there be the *pravāraṇā* ceremony?

How can there be the calculation of seniority (*paryāya*)? If one were to perform the *anupraskandaka-vāsa* (mental dwelling) alone, the Vinaya regulations state that this is not permitted for anyone;
therefore, the method of dwelling through formal declaration (*pratimukha-vāsa*) must not be omitted. It differs only in that one does not inquire about relying on another person. Thus it should be.
The presiding master of the Dharma should first enter the retreat (*varṣā*) himself, and only thereafter accept another’s entry into retreat.
(If the person he is addressing is not among his disciples, they should each perform a single prostration, and then stand facing one another and say:)
"Venerable sir, please attend to me with one-pointed mind. I, the bhikṣu [Name], now enter the three-month summer retreat at this [Name] monastery.
(Recite three times. The person being addressed says: 'Excellent. (The presiding master replies: 'So be it.'"
(They should still exchange one bow with each other. If the person being addressed is a disciple, the difference lies solely in receiving the prostration.

When a senior monk (*upādhyāya*) enters the rains retreat (*varṣā*) toward the presiding master of the Dharma, the response regarding the Dharma is likewise. Because both parties are proficient in the Vinaya scriptures, they do not rely on [the status of] the person.
If one were to still enter the retreat based on the person [rather than the Dharma], one would fall into the rank of a mere disciple. As stated in the Vinaya.)
As for those who have been explained: an *ācārya* who bestows the scriptures—even if one hears from him only a single four-line verse—is called a "teacher.
An *ācārya* upon whom one relies—even if it is for only a single night—is called a "reliant teacher" (*niśrayācārya*). How much more so, then, if one relies on them for ninety days?
How could there not be at least one dharma by which to provide instruction? If one does not treat [the preceptor] with the etiquette due to a disciple, it contravenes the Vinaya regulations.
If [the preceptor] is able to master the Piṇi-piṭaka (Vinaya-piṭaka) without obstruction, then requiring him to perform the rites of a disciple might not be appropriate for him.
Therefore, by observing the rains retreat in this manner, both human sentiment and the Buddha’s regulations will not be in conflict; this is what is proper.

If one who performs *saṃghakarma* does not know what is permitted or prohibited, or what constitutes upholding or transgressing the precepts, then even if they are a senior elder (*sthavira*), their case shall not be treated as equivalent;
it should follow the subsequent example).
Next, regarding the basis of reliance, one must rely on a person.
As for relying on a person, it refers to a senior elder (*sthavira*) who is ignorant of the Vinaya and his disciples. The *Mūla-vinaya* states:
"During the summer retreat, one should rely on a fifth-level Vinaya master: first, one who recites from the introduction of the precepts up to the thirty rules; second..."

1. Reciting the *Śīlaskandha* (the Preface to the Precepts) up to the ninety offenses. 2. Extensively reciting the *Vinaya* of the precepts. 3. Extensively reciting the *Vinaya* of both divisions (*Dvibhāga*).
4. Extensively reciting the *Vinaya*. If one violates these, it is a *pāyattika* offense. At other times, one should rely on the four types of *vinayadhara* (masters of discipline);
to violate this is a *duṣkṛta* offense. The *Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya* states: "If a bhikṣu is well-versed in the Tripiṭaka and has attained [realization]..."

One who has mastered the three knowledges (*tisro vidyāḥ*) and eliminated the three stains (*trimala*), yet has not completed five years of summer retreat (*pañca-varṣa*), must still rely upon a preceptor.

Likewise, one who is eighty years of age and has completed sixty years of summer retreat, yet has never recited the *Prātimokṣa-sūtra* and does not understand its meaning, [must also rely upon a preceptor].
One must also rely upon a junior [preceptor] and practice the duties of a disciple, with the sole exception of performing prostrations. The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states:
"If one has received the precepts for many years yet does not know the laws of a bhikṣu, he should remain dependent on another for as long as his life lasts."
Thus one knows that such persons must all rely upon others for their *an-gi* (the summer retreat).
(The preceptor then takes his seat; the one observing the *an-gi* performs a single prostration, kneels with lowered body, joins the palms, and makes the following announcement:)
"Venerable sir, please attend to me with a focused mind. I, the bhikṣu [Name], now enter the three-month summer retreat at this [Name] monastery.

(Recite this three times. The teacher says: 'I know; do not be negligent. (The disciple replies: 'I shall uphold it. (According to the intent of the Vinaya, the preceptor should ask: 'Upon which master who upholds the Vinaya do you rely?'"
(Answer: I rely on Master [Name] (upper) and [Name] (lower). (The Master says: If you have doubts, you should go and ask him. (Answer: Yes.
(1) After prostrating once and rising to exchange greetings, the second person enters through the left cheek-door from the center, performs prostrations, and makes the formal announcement as above.
Having completed the summer retreat (*an-gyo*), he exits through the right cheek-door from the center and proceeds to the place where the daily recitation is held.

When the *vinaya-dhara* (Venerable Leader) and the secretary see him approaching, they should ask: "Under which master did you receive the precepts? In which year? Was it spring, summer, autumn, or winter?"
Regarding that particular year: how many *lǎ* (years of seniority) has he? One summer’s *an-jū* (rainy-season retreat) constitutes one *lǎ*.

How much has he practiced mindfulness of the Buddha (*niàn fó*), performed prostrations (*lǐ-pài*), and recited scriptures (*chí-sòng*)? In which hall (*táng*) or in which private cell (*dān*) does he reside?

After he has answered these questions as above, wait for the record-keeper (*shū-jì*) to annotate them before departing. For other members of the *an-jū*, ask and answer in the same manner and have them annotated. This is what is meant by the "sequential arrangement" (*xù-cì ān*).
Regarding those who remain: first, the Hall of the Precepts and the Hall for Learning the Precepts; next, the heads of the external quarters, each with their own individual single beds;

and finally, those residing separately enter the summer retreat. The procedures for small groups are all based on the above, with the sole exception that the two characters "śrāmaṇera" (novice) are substituted.
If the affairs of the permanent residence are numerous, those within the hall should yield several seats to them to settle first. If there is no such opportunity, one must...

In this sequence, one must not take up the chamber-pot. If there are many people in the *varṣā* (rainy season retreat), one should appoint a leader or an elder (*sthavira*) to perform the ritual at several locations.
Although the individuals facing each other differ, the name of the *vinaya-dhara* (master of discipline) mentioned in the text remains the same.
Once the internal and external *varṣā* are completed, the person in charge of the duties shall instruct the striking of the bell three times for the assembly.
Gather before the Buddha Hall and perform three prostrations to the Buddha. After turning to inquire after Vajrapāṇi, proceed to the abbot’s quarters and prostrate three times to the *ho-shang*.
Once the assembly has divided into left and right ranks, and the *ho-shang* has exhorted the great multitude, the leader shall speak.

The assembly lines up facing upward to pay their respects to the Abbot with three prostrations. (The Abbot says: "One prostration. (Or he may say: "Exempt from the ritual. (Having spoken, they each return.
They wait for the kneeling recitation before inspecting the quarters. For those entering the summer retreat later, they perform the rites as they arrive;
the text is the same as above, differing only in the word "later").

4. Explanation of the Method for the Daily Recitation (The following day, the *vinaya-dhara* [Venerable Leader], together with the *karmadāna* [Secretary], prepares the daily recitation register. There is also a sequential order for writing it down:
first the bell and wooden board hall, then the Hall of Training, followed by the heads of the external quarters and the various individual practitioners, as well as all the *śrāmaṇeras*. At...)
Under each person's name, record the number of recitations of the Buddha’s name and the number of prostrations performed; write the number "one" at the top, or specify a particular hall or quarters.

Having completed this sequence, the administrative official (zhishi) shall take the register to go through the inner and outer precincts, as well as each quarters, to verify the number of persons present, so that items may be inspected during the *pravāraṇā* ceremony. Should anyone have reasons to leave the boundary, they must notify those coming and going.
This is done to ensure that the members of the community dwell together in harmony. Fifth is the method for recording the seniority of ordination (*pravrajyā-varṣa*) according to sequence:

once the daily record book has been completed, one must again write out the plaque indicating the order of seniority; first, write the four large characters "An-ju-la-ci" (安居臘次, *Anju-ratsuji*, meaning "Seniority of the Summer Retreat").
This serves as the title. The heading is written upon the face of the ordination register (*karmavācanā*).

Beneath each person’s name, it is clearly noted the year, the period of ordination, and whether they have completed the summer retreat (*varṣa*) or not, from the first to the last, with each entry concluded in sequence. A further section is written for those who entered the later retreat (*paścimikā varṣā*).

Furthermore, there are those who have received the *parivāsa* penance for a second offense, as well as bodhisattva novices (*śrāmaṇera*), those under the five precepts, and those under the ten precepts.
Thereafter, those who enter the summer retreat (an-gu) shall ascend the seats as they arrive; the formalities are as previously described.
However, it is essential to clearly note the dates so that the duration of the days may be fulfilled, lest one incur the fault of violating the summer retreat (bā-śa).

When the six classes of beings were dwelling in their respective abodes according to the Dharma at that time, there were no persons upon whom they could rely. Not knowing what they should do, they went to inform the World-Honored One.

The Buddha said: "If there is no person upon whom one can rely, one should perform the *anāśraya* (non-reliance) *varṣā* by means of mental resolve. [One should] mentally rely on that [person], while verbally expressing one's own situation; this does not mean remaining silent."
...and so forth). On the seventh day, one obtains a place for going and returning. One relies on a person from afar (when the time arrives, one performs the ritual with full decorum).
"I, the bhikṣu [Name], now rely on the saṃghārāma at [Place] for the three-month summer retreat (*varṣā*).

I rely from afar on the Vinaya Master [Name]" (recite this three times; this method of mental recitation is permitted only for the *pūrvavārṣika* [early] retreat, and it cannot be taken as a precedent for the *madhyama* [middle] or *paścimavārṣika* [late] retreats).
The Seven Rules for Requesting a Teacher of Reliance (following the preceding example).
The *Karmavācanā* on Receiving Ordination states: "One who has newly received full ordination should always rely upon the upādhyāya and comply with his instructions."
While studying and upholding the *vinaya*, there was a bhikṣu whose preceptor (*upādhyāya*) passed away, or who had abandoned the path, or who resolved to go beyond the boundary of the monastery.
Because there was no one to provide instruction, he committed various violations of the precepts and engaged in improper conduct. The Buddha said: "I allow that there be an *ācārya*;
you should seek one for dependence (*niśraya*), following the same rules as for a preceptor. An *ācārya* should look after his disciple as..."
The disciple should regard the preceptor as a father; they should together offer mutual respect and attentive care.
In this way, the True Dharma will abide for a long time, increasing and expanding. (One who seeks formal reliance should properly cultivate dignified deportment and make the following request:)
"Venerable sir, please attend to me with one-pointed mind. I, [Name], now request the Venerable sir to act as my preceptor (niśraya). May the Venerable sir grant me his preceptorship.
I shall dwell depending upon the Venerable sir. (Recite this three times. Having accepted the request, he should reply:)
"It is well; I shall provide you with dependence (*niśraya*). Do not be negligent. (The disciple should respond: "So be it.
(Having prostrated once, he rises. If one has completed five years of residence but is unable to recite the *Prātimokṣa* or the *Karmavācanā*, they must remain in dependence for as long as they live.
The method of service is like that of a *Vidyādhara*. [The two characters "Bhikṣu" at the end should be added according to the context].)
○ Chapter Five: Repentance and Cultivating Purity (Two Methods).
First, the Method of Personally Examining the Precepts:

For more than ten days prior to the *pravāraṇā*, one should strike the bell for the Seven-Day Buddha-Mindfulness Retreat according to the established regulations of one’s former preceptor. At the beginning...
On the day before the ceremony begins, one first performs repentance to become pure so as to enter the Buddha-recitation hall.
This clearly demonstrates that pure precepts are the cause and the Pure Land is the fruit; wishing to purify the Buddha-land, one must first purify one’s own body and mind.
This is the Master’s method of repentance (*sāṃmā*), which differs from the fortnightly ritual.

(On the afternoon of this day, the *sāṃghāṭī* plaque for the ritual of confession (*kṣamāpana*) is hung. The officiant orders a *śrāmaṇera* or a junior *bhikṣu* to sweep and sprinkle the site, arrange the seats, and light the lamps.
When the time arrives, the wooden mallet is struck—this refers to striking the bell three times, or alternatively, fifty-four times.
Upon hearing this, the assembly each dons the sevenfold robe (*saptaka-cīvara*), takes up their ritual implements, and with solemn decorum proceeds to the performance of the rite.)
Once the inner and outer [attendants] have assembled, one person holding incense and another following behind with a *qǐng* (sounding gong) proceed.

Furthermore, there must be four, six, or at most eight persons at the head; they go to the Abbot’s quarters (*fangzhāng*) to invite the Master. The one holding the incense walks through the central gate.

The others enter through the side door and stand in order to the left and right. When the *hōshō* (Preceptor) sounds the *rinkyō* (leading chime), they immediately emerge from the *warishitsu* (sleeping quarters).
Upon reaching the front of the *kōi* (public seat), the one who invites performs three prostrations toward it; the *hōshō* replies with one prostration.

Finally, the Preceptor walks first with the *rinkyō* following behind, while the incense-bearer precedes the *hōshō*. Arriving at the place of ritual, if [the image] is that of the Buddha, one performs three prostrations.

Having performed the prostrations, he ascends the seat. Regarding this seat, it is traditionally not provided with offerings for the Buddha; however, if one consults the text on repentance (*chànhuì wén*), which states:
"If there are those who have transgressed, they should confess and repent before the Triple Gem," then providing offerings is not improper.

Once the leader has finished offering incense, the assembly forms ranks, performs three prostrations with their heads to the ground, and exchanges greetings. Only then do they divide into groups and take their positions.
Next, the method for presenting the daily recitation according to the ritual protocol:

(The person receiving the charge shall first have another person carry the daily recitation ledger. Then, emerging from the assembly, they shall remove their shoes, spread out the great mat (*kaṭhina*), and with utmost sincerity, perform three prostrations.
Having offered greetings, they shall kneel long on both knees, holding the daily recitation ledger in their hands, and speak in a loud voice:)
He speaks as follows: "I, [Name],
having been commissioned by the Upādhyāya to oversee the daily recitations of the assembly and maintain the registers,
now report to the Upādhyāya that the ninety-day period is drawing to a close."
(The attendant receives the daily practice ledger and presents it at the seat. The *vinaya-dhara* stands and performs three prostrations. The *ho-shang* responds with one prostration.

[The *vinaya-dhara*] rises, adjusts his robes, bows in greeting, and returns to his position. This is not a formal assembly because the offender must come forward personally to confess their transgression.

After the *ho-shang* has briefly recorded the daily practice in the ledger and finished his exhortation, if there are those who wish to disclose their faults, the person in charge of the matter should...)
Having clearly identified each instance of the offenses one by one, and having ensured that each individual has completed their repentance, only then may the *pravāraṇā* (self-indulgence) proceed.
Once the inquiry into purity (*pāriśuddhi*) has been conducted, the assembly shall line up facing upward, pay their respects, and withdraw.
Section Six: The Chapter on the Invitation at the End of the Rains Retreat (Eleven Dharmas).

First, the Method for Gathering *Kuśa* Grass as Prescribed (On the fourteenth day of the seventh month, the administrative official shall have a *śrāmaṇera* or a lay attendant gather auspicious *kuśa* grass and select it).
Discard those that are withered and yellow, and take only those that are fresh and excellent. Tie twelve leaves together to form a bundle; if it is a leap year, there shall be one additional leaf.
Prepare the number of bundles according to the number of people—using two trays, four trays, or eight trays if there are many people.
The counting sticks (*śalākā*) should be prepared in the same manner. Once they have been prepared according to these regulations, they may be used as needed.
2. The Procedure for Requesting the Consent (*chanda*) by Questioning (Having received the board at dawn on the fifteenth day, one stands before the hall or in the Buddha Hall facing the assembly.
The Elder should speak as follows):
Venerable Saṃgha, listen. Today is the fifteenth day of the waxing moon. The community of monks has assembled at such-and-such a place for the *pravāraṇā* (one recitation).
[Having exchanged greetings, each returns to their own place. If the *pravāraṇā* is held during the day, it is announced before the main meal or the light meal.

If there are matters concerning the Triple Gem or other circumstances involving illness, it is permitted to grant one's consent (*chanda*). One capable person should be appointed to hold this consent within the boundary (*sīmā*).

One receives [the *chanda*] from each respective place according to the size of the boundary. If one requires someone to convey the *chanda* during the night, one should appoint one or two people as companions.
The *Vinayamātṛkā-śāstra* states: "There are five methods for granting the *chanda* for the *pravāraṇā*:

first, 'Today the Saṃgha performs the *pravāraṇā*; I grant my *chanda* to the Saṃgha for the *pravāraṇā*'; second, 'I inform you that I shall perform the *pravāraṇā*'; third, 'For my sake, perform the *pravāraṇā*'; fourth..."
If one is unable to speak, one may grant the *pravāraṇā* by making a gesture with the hand; this also constitutes granting the *pravāraṇā*.
Fifth, even if the speech is not fully intelligible, it still constitutes granting the *pravāraṇā*. These are called the five methods for granting the desire (*chanda*) for the *pravāraṇā*.
This is the first method for granting the desire; one should address the recipient and speak as follows:

"Venerable sir, please attend to me with one-pointed mindfulness. I, the bhikṣu [Name], regarding the formal matter of the Saṃgha, grant my consent for the *pravāraṇā* (self-examination). [Recite once.

(The Vinaya states: If there are reasons such as the Buddha, the Dharma, or illness, one may change the wording when speaking; having thus received the consent in each respective place, one then returns to the hall as before.)"

The Method for Spreading the Seats and Inviting the Preceptor (The *karmadāna* shall instruct a junior bhikṣu or a śrāmaṇera to arrange the necessary implements at the place where the ritual is performed).

The Fundamental Vinaya states: "One should perform the *pravāraṇā* ceremony in an open space. The person in charge of ritual affairs should observe the number of those in the assembly to appropriately prepare mats and arrange seats for the monks.
Furthermore, an image of Śākyamuni Buddha must be enshrined in the center with its face upward;
in the upper left corner, an image of Vaiśravaṇa is to be enshrined, also facing upward. Incense and flowers must be arranged in rows, and lamps and candles must burn brightly. To the left...
To the right, spread the seats for the assembly of monks. In the upper left corner, arrange the seat for the *upādhyāya*. Within this space, set up two low tables.
Place a grass mat and a tray before the front low table and cover them with fresh flowers. Place the counting-tray (*śalākā-paṭṭa*) on the rear low table.
He also covers it with fresh flowers. Once the preparations are complete, those who have business elsewhere return. The *mudgara* (wooden mallet) is struck to assemble the Saṃgha.

This is according to the ritual for reciting the *Prātimokṣa*. The bell is struck so that the great assembly may take notice; each person dons the seven-fold robe (*saptaka-cīvara*) and holds their sitting mat (*niṣīdana*).

With dignified and solemn deportment, they proceed to the place where the rite is performed. They prostrate once before the Buddha, arrange themselves in order according to seniority, and stand in their places. The official in charge observes them.
When the assembly has gathered together, the leader holds the incense, followed by two people with the *yin-qing* (guiding chime).

Then, four, six, or eight *jiezhang* (precept elders) go to the Abbot’s quarters to invite the Master. The one holding the incense proceeds through the central gate, while the others enter from the side.

The Abbot emerges from his quarters and proceeds to the position of honor. The one who performs the invitation prostrates three times—or once—and then walks ahead of the procession to the place where the ritual is performed.
The incense-bearer stands at the rear of the lower-ranking monks. The one who performed the invitation returns to his own position.
Two people holding *yin-gheng* (small hand-chimes) stand before the Buddha. When the Abbot arrives, he first performs a single inquiry-greeting (*wen-xun*), then kneels and offers incense.
Having finished, he rises and bows once more before descending. Standing in the center and facing upward, he performs three prostrations to the Buddha.
The attendant stands behind the Master (Heshang). Once the prostrations are complete, the two lead the Master to the presence of Weituo.

Upon arriving, the Master first performs one bow of inquiry, offers incense with three discernments, and bows again twice. The Master then turns his body and ascends the stairs, returning to his position to stand. [The attendants] lead him.

"Please, attendants, each return to your respective positions. Once the leader has offered incense, the assembly shall line up facing upward and perform three prostrations with utmost sincerity to the Buddha. [The leader says:]"
Turning toward the lower direction, he pays his respects to Weituo (three times). Turning toward the upper direction, he prostrates three times to the Abbot.

(The Abbot says: "Prostrate to the Buddha" (or: "One prostration to the Buddha"). Having finished bowing, the Abbot sits down and says: "Each person take their place in order. (Each person removes their sandals, places a mat upon it, and sits in the full lotus position.)
Fourth, the assembly gathers to distinguish the Dharma (After the great assembly has sat, once the Preceptor has finished his instruction, he first performs the preliminary rites and then asks):
"Is the Saṃgha assembled? (Answer: "The Saṃgha is assembled. "Is it in harmony? "It is in harmony. "Have those who have not received full ordination departed? (Answer:
"There are none among them who have not received full ordination. "Are there any bhikṣus who have not come and have sent their *chanda* (consent)?

(The bearer of the *chanda* joins his palms while seated and answers: "There are. (He then rises from his seat, stands in the center, bows once toward the upper direction, kneels for a long time, joins his palms, and says:)
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen. I, [Name], many bhikṣus, have received their consent (*chanda*). Regarding that legal matter of the Saṃgha, I grant my consent for the *pravāraṇā* (self-examination).
(Recite once. The response is: "Excellent. (Answer: "So be it. (Bowing once and rising, return to one's seat. The Upādhyāya asks:)
Who has sent a bhikṣuṇī to request the invitation for the *pravāraṇā* regarding the three matters of what has been seen, heard, or suspected? (If there is none, one should answer:

"There is no bhikṣuṇī here to come and request the invitation for the *pravāraṇā* regarding the three matters of what has been seen, heard, or suspected. (If someone has newly entered the monastery and wishes to participate in the ritual with sympathetic joy, they should answer in this manner.)

No bhikṣuṇīs have come here to request the *pravāraṇā* ceremony; there are only those who pay homage at the feet of the monks. (The presiding officer says: "Call them here. (The administrator calls out: "All bhikṣuṇīs, come forth!

(Upon hearing their names called, the bhikṣuṇīs take up their sitting cloths (*niṣīdana*) and advance with solemn decorum. The *karmadāna* calls out: "Line up all together facing upward and unfold your large sitting cloths.
Upon hearing the sound of the *ghaṇṭā*, prostrate three times. Exchange greetings. Kneel long. Join your palms."
The Upādhyāya briefly proclaims the instructions:

The Chapter on *Pravāraṇā*:

"Pravāraṇā" means that when one has committed a transgression but does not personally recognize one's own fault, one allows others to point it out clearly, so as to reform one's errors and start anew.

The Eight Rules of Respect: 1. A nun of even a hundred years' seniority, upon seeing a newly ordained bhikṣu, must prostrate and inquire after his well-being.

2. She must not revile or slander a bhikṣu. 3. She must not expose the faults of a bhikṣu. 4. When a śikṣamāṇā has completed her training in the precepts, she should receive full ordination from the great assembly of monks (bhikṣusaṃgha).
5. If a nun commits a saṃghāvaśeṣa offense, she must undergo penance before an assembly consisting of three groups of monks.
Sixth: One shall practice the *mānatva* penance for half a month. Seventh: During the half-monthly *poṣadha*, one must seek an instructor from within the Saṃgha.
Eighth: One should not observe the rains retreat (*varṣā*) where there are no monks. Ninth: Upon concluding the rains retreat, one must seek an instructor from within the Saṃgha.
The five qualities of one who reproves for faults: namely, being without attachment, hatred, fear, or delusion; and knowing whether the *pravāraṇā* has been performed or not yet performed.

The five qualities of one who performs the *pravāraṇā*: namely, knowing the proper time, speaking according to reality, being gentle, acting for the benefit of others, and possessing a mind of loving-kindness.

this makes eighteen. The *antarvāsaka* (inner robe) is likewise permitted to be made by either the method of cutting into patches or the method of sewing leaves together; these two constitute the second category.

Tenth: There are twenty-two types of the seven robes according to the Dharma. These consist of eighteen types of the *saṃghāṭī* (great robe) and four types of the five robes—namely, the cut-and-sewn (*khaṇḍa*), the gathered-leaf (*saṃpuṭa*), the stitched-leaf (*sīvana*), and the seamless (*ekata*)—which together constitute twenty-two types.

The *saṃghāṭī* has six types according to the Dharma: namely, the five robes (*pañca-cīvara*) with four methods of formal ritual action (*karmavācanā*), and the seven robes (*sapta-cīvara*) with two methods of formal ritual action; these constitute the six types.

The Initial Procedure for Surveying the Boundary Markers (based on the *Vinaya-vibhaṅga*). Generally speaking, wherever a bhikṣu resides, he must not dwell without a defined boundary (*sīmā*).
If one violates this regulation, the ritual procedure will not be valid, and the Saṃgha incurs an offense. If a bhikṣu relies upon a city, town, or village, within its jurisdiction...
When monks residing in a monastery wish to perform the monastic rites and first establish a great boundary (*mahā-sīmā*), the elder (*sthavira*) shall first measure out the limits.

He shall then instruct the administrative officers (*karmadāna*) to erect boundary markers at the four cardinal directions. If there is a training ground (*sīmāntara*), it shall consist of three layers, with one layer on the innermost side.

The innermost circle constitutes the boundary mark for the exterior of the *śīmaṇḍala* (precept enclosure). The middle circle constitutes the boundary mark for the interior of the *mahāśīma* (great boundary).
The outermost circle constitutes the boundary mark for the exterior of the *mahāśīma*. If there is no *śīmaṇḍala*, there is only one circle serving as the exterior boundary mark.

Once these marks have been established, a number of bhikṣus corresponding to the extent of that territory must go to agree upon and fix the period [of the retreat]. First, they should collectively observe the boundary markers and proceed to the exterior.
Regarding the boundaries (*sīmā*): the official in charge of affairs should point out and say, "This is the outer boundary-mark at such-and-such a corner of the Great Boundary (*mahāsīmā*);

Everyone must clearly remember this without forgetting, so that when the sound of the proclamation is heard at the time of the ceremony, one may recall it in the mind and the corresponding signs will appear accordingly).

The recitation of the precepts and the dissolution of the *anāpatti-sīmā* (the boundary for not losing one's robe) are concluded. Since the Saṃgha remains silent, it is accepted; this matter is thus maintained.

Next is the dissolution of the *mahāsīmā* (great boundary). As the Vinaya states: "At that time, the bhikṣus desired to enlarge [the boundary] or to narrow it. The Buddha said: 'If you wish to alter it, [you must proceed as follows...']"

First, explain the preceding boundary. Then, determine its extent—whether broad or narrow—according to one’s intention. The procedure for striking the gong to assemble the community and the ritual for the question-and-answer session shall all be performed as previously described.
The *karmadāna* (the officiant) should explain it in this manner.
Venerable Saṃgha, listen. These bhikṣus residing in this dwelling place share the same residence and the same recitation of the Prātimokṣa.
If the time is right for the Saṃgha, and the Saṃgha is willing to grant its consent, I shall announce the dissolution of the boundary (*sīmā-bandha*). This is the formal motion (*jñapti*).
Venerable Saṃgha, listen. The monks residing in this dwelling place share the same residence and the same recitation of the *Prātimokṣa*. Now, the boundary is being dissolved.
Those elders who consent to the dissolution of the boundary for those sharing the same residence and the same recitation of the *Prātimokṣa*, let them remain silent.

Whoever does not consent should speak. The Saṃgha has consented; it has heard [the proposal] that the boundary for those sharing the same residence and the same recitation of the *Prātimokṣa* is hereby dissolved. The Saṃgha is in agreement.
Because you have endured in silence, this matter is thus upheld.

(This *karmavācanā* does not solely dissolve the *mahā-sīmā*. Should there be other boundaries, such as the *acīvara-bhūmi* [the area where robes may not be left] or the *pariṣaṇḍa* [surrounding wall], these various boundaries are all dissolved.
Why? Because the text contains no restrictive limitation. If one were to say that it dissolves only the *mahā-sīmā*, then [the others] would not be dissolved.)

General explanation: One must explain each case individually, as the texts differ. The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states: "When the great boundary (*mahā-sīmā*) is relinquished, the boundary for not being separated from one's robes (*acīvarāpavādana-sīmā*) is also relinquished;
however, if the boundary for not being separated from one's robes is relinquished, the great boundary is not relinquished. It further states:
"If a boundary has previously been established and not relinquished, one may not establish another boundary [over it]."

Next is the procedure for dissolving the *sīmā* (boundary). Since it was established based on specific conditions, it must be dissolved when subsequent conditions arise; this is why it is provided here as a model for practical application.

All ritual protocols for assembling the Sangha are to be conducted exactly as described above. However, as there is no explicit textual authority in the Vinaya regarding this, the Southern Vinaya masters have established this by analogy with various methods for dissolution.
This is also cited by way of analogy. The principle is sound and the phrasing is smooth; one who performs the ritual should understand it as follows):
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen. The Saṃgha now assembles at this dwelling place to dissolve the *sīmā* (boundary). If the time is right for the Saṃgha, may the Saṃgha grant its consent."
Dissolving the *śīmaṇḍala*. The announcement is as follows: "Venerable Saṃgha, listen. The Saṃgha now assembles at this residence to dissolve the *śīmaṇḍala*.
Those elders who consent to the Saṃgha dissolving the *śīmaṇḍala* at this residence, remain silent. Whoever does not consent, please speak. The Saṃgha has consented to dissolve the *śīmaṇḍala*."
It is concluded. Because the Saṃgha has consented by remaining silent, this matter is thus upheld.
All other procedures are the same as above.

○ Second, the Section on Receiving Days to Leave the Boundary (The receiving of days for the *varṣā* is not fixed as to whether it occurs or not; therefore, it is categorized under "Non-Seasonal" [procedures], which consist of nine rules).

Regarding the initial striking of the wooden mallet to assemble the community, the Vinaya states that the Buddha said: "If a bhikṣu in retreat encounters circumstances such as matters concerning the Buddha, the Dharma, or the Saṅgha;

or if he is summoned by his parents or donors for the sake of receiving the precepts, performing repentance, and so forth; or if he must attend to the sick and seek medicine, resolve doubts, or request the Dharma."

Regarding such matters, if one cannot return on that very day, permission is granted to depart for seven days. If one cannot return within seven days, permission is granted to depart for half a month.
If one cannot return within half a month, one shall receive permission to depart for one month. These three types of receiving [permission] for a set number of days do not include the nights.
The first is a *pratimokṣa-karman* (formal act performed before an individual), while the latter two are both *jñapti* (motions) according to the rules of the Saṃgha.

Second, regarding the *karmavācanā* (formal ritual): if there are causes and conditions such as those mentioned above that necessitate receiving [ordination] within the Saṃgha, one should first inform the person in charge and notify the *upādhyāya*.

Once this has been done, one should then appeal to the internal and external assemblies to demonstrate that, as members of the same boundary (*sīmā*) living together, everyone knows of one’s comings and goings, and that one is not departing the boundary due to unwholesome causes and conditions.

If that monastery lacks a designated ordination site (*sīmā*) or great boundary (*mahāsīmā*), when the time arrives, the administrator should appoint a capable person to solicit the consent (*chanda*) of the assembly;
thereafter, he should instruct them to strike the *gandī* drum (or, according to the *Kṣamā* method, to beat the drum). Upon hearing it, the great assembly [assembles].

Each person shall adjust their deportment and proceed to the place where the ritual is to be performed. Once the assembly of monks has gathered together, the administrator shall go to the Abbot’s quarters and inform the attendant, requesting that the Preceptor come to the place of the ritual, speaking as follows: (Thus he speaks.)
The assembly bows upward in prostration to the Abbot. (The Abbot should respond: "Exempt from ceremony" (or say: "One bow.

(When the ritual is concluded, the assembly divides into ranks. The administrative officers instruct the recipient of the precepts to step out from the assembly. He takes his place in the center facing upward and spreads his ritual implements.)
[The Master] calls out.
First, one prostrates three times to the Preceptor.
The Preceptor says, "I too am counted among the ranks of monks. The assembly joins their palms in unison.

2. The Method for Presenting One’s Circumstances and Requesting Leave (Having prostrated, one should first state one’s circumstances. Since there are no words for requesting leave in the Vinaya, those who receive a formal extension of their period of stay should speak aloud to the assembly, saying:)

I require to leave the boundary for a period of half a month or one month. I beseech the Upādhyāya, the Saṃgha, and the Ācāryas to grant their compassion.
(Having finished speaking, he performs one prostration, rises, and makes inquiries. He stands to one side. If it concerns matters for the permanent residence, he need not go;

this need not be stated. If there are others who have received the same *uposatha* day but their affairs differ, or if their days do not coincide, they likewise perform a prostration toward the assembly as above.
Having presented their own reasons for leaving the boundary, they separately announce the *karmavācanā*. This is because of the departure.)

The realm (*dhātu*) is the same. Because there is a difference in the conditions and the time, if the matter and the time were both identical, then for two or three people, one round of the formal act (*karmavācanā*) would suffice;
for four, five, or six people, two rounds of the announcement (*jñapti*) would be required.

I shall convey their *chanda-karman*. (Recite once more. Good. (Answer: "So be it. (One prostrates, rises, prepares the ritual implements, inquires after the health of the assembly, and returns to one's place. Hereafter, all shall follow this procedure. The officiant asks again:)
The Saṃgha is now in harmony. What is to be done? (Answer: The formal act (*karmavācanā*) for receiving a half-month’s leave to go outside the boundary.
Regarding the four methods of deliberation and approval:
having performed the preliminary procedures, the Preceptor and the Great Assembly shall deliberate upon the disposition and the circumstances of the person receiving the leave. Truly...

If it is not the case that [the offense] is unreal, one should grant a half-month or a month’s period according to the circumstances. One must not, out of personal sentiment, treat the Dharma lightly;

once the decision is finalized, the Upādhyāya says: “The *karmavācanā* (formal ritual) shall be performed. Upon hearing this, the *karman*-officiant should rise from the assembly, perform a single prostration toward the upper direction, or cease if he is exempted. This is the formal announcement (*jñapti*).

Venerable Saṃgha, listen. The bhikṣu [Name] has received the seven-day leave; for the sake of a certain matter, he shall go outside the boundary for up to half a month and return here to observe the rains retreat.
Whichever elders consent, let the Saṃgha grant permission for the bhikṣu [Name].

The procedure for receiving the *saptāha-atireka* (seven-day extension) rule: [If a monk] intends to go outside the boundary for half a month or one month for a certain matter, and will return to this very place to observe the rains retreat, he should remain silent. Whoever does not consent should speak. The Sangha has consented;

it is heard that the monk [Name] has received the seven-day extension rule to go outside the boundary for half a month or one month for a certain matter, and shall return to this very place to complete the rains retreat. The Sangha—[consents].
Because he has consented by remaining silent, this matter is thus upheld.
(After the *karmavācanā* is completed, the officiant should still perform one prostration toward the assembly; if the matter is waived, it stops there.
The person receiving the day-off [from the assembly] should perform three prostrations or one salutation toward the assembly and stand to one side before them.)
The Preceptor says regarding the five cautions for departing the boundary: "Although this is indeed the Dharma, you have received a half-month leave.

Though your body is outside the boundary, your mind must constantly remain mindful of being within the boundary. Do not be negligent; perform your daily recitations as usual. Once your business is concluded—"
One must immediately return to the boundary; it is not permitted to insist on returning only after a fixed period has expired.

If, having finished one's business, one intentionally remains outside and fails to return, thereby wasting time in vain, this is called being "under the rains" (varṣā) without having successfully completed the retreat (anupagata-varṣā). It does not constitute a valid *anvārambhaṇa* (rainy-season retreat).
(When he has finished speaking. The one who received the day [of ordination] should again leave the assembly to pay respects to the Preceptor and the Great Assembly. Then the administrator says:
"The Great Assembly prostrates to the Preceptor. (The Preceptor says: "You need not prostrate."
(Each person disperses in turn. When the person receiving the day-off leaves the boundary, they first go to the branch hall and announce:
"I am leaving the boundary on such-and-such a day. This is done so that their arrival may be clearly verified upon their return, thereby providing evidence for authentication.)

Regarding the *Vinaya-śāstra* on receiving [the *poṣadha*] through a formal procedure (*pratyekamukha*) for six days, it only permits the reception of a seven-day period; there is no authentic tradition of the True Dharma [extending beyond this].

Within the formal motion (*jñapti-karman*), there is likewise no logical flaw. If, due to circumstances, one is unable to return on the same day after six, five, or even just one day, [the procedure remains valid].
All should perform this rite to receive the day; it does not extend into the night. Once the matter is concluded, one must return immediately and may not linger.

At that time, there was a bhikṣu who had gone beyond the boundary and did not know before whom he should perform the rite. The Buddha said: "One should perform the rite in the presence of a single bhikṣu.
If no bhikṣu is available, one should receive it from the other four assemblies."
The person receiving the day [of ordination] should first inform the *upādhyāya* and, once his assessment and permission have been granted, proceed to the place of the *bhikṣu*.
Having performed the full ritual prostrations as before, he should first declare his circumstances and subsequently present the formal petition.
If the person he addresses is of equal seniority or a junior, he should stand facing them while making the petition; if they are a senior (*sthavira*), [he should remain seated].
Regarding the aforementioned precept: having prostrated and knelt with the right knee on the ground, join the palms and say:

"Venerable sir, please attend to me with one-pointed mind. I, the bhikṣu [Name], now receive the seven-day leave to go outside the boundary for the sake of [specific] business, returning here to observe the rains retreat.
I inform the Venerable sir so that he may know. (Recite this three times. The person addressed says: "Well done. (The respondent replies: "So be it."
(One prostrates once and rises. After the aforementioned signal has been given, one may then depart the boundary).
7. The Rules for Receiving the *Saptarātra* (Seven-Night) Permission.
In the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, the Buddha said: "If a bhikṣu, having received the *saptarātra* permission, departs outside the boundary and [the seven nights] have not yet expired..."

Upon returning, if the matter is not yet concluded, one is permitted to receive the "remaining-night" (*śeṣarātra*) leave. One should perform the ritual with full decorum and pay homage, making the following announcement:
"Venerable Sir, please attend to me with a single mind. I, the bhikṣu [Name], have received the seven-night rule;

such-and-such nights remain. I now receive permission to depart. (The one addressed says: "Very well" (one response). (The petitioner replies: "So be it" (one prostration and departure). If the circumstances of the matter are different, then one should not receive this leave; rather, another procedure must be performed.

Regarding the method for a monk dwelling alone to mentally resolve upon the number of days [of the *pravāraṇā*] according to the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*: it permits a monk living in solitude to mentally resolve upon the days. He should properly maintain his dignified deportment and perform the mental resolution with verbal expression as follows:
I, the bhikṣu [Name], now receive the seven-day leave to go beyond the boundary for the sake of [a certain] matter,
returning to this very place to observe the rains retreat (three times).

(When departing the boundary, one should personally record the number of days; having completed the business, one must return immediately. One must take the Dharma as paramount and remain mindful of being within the boundary;
one may not decide for oneself what is permitted or prohibited. This constitutes a semblance of the rains retreat, which has the name but lacks the reality.)
9. The Procedure for Receiving the Remaining Night (*śeṣarātra*) Designation.

The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states: If a bhikṣu, having mentally resolved to receive the seven-night designation, goes outside the boundary but returns before the period has expired and his business remains unfinished, the Buddha said:
"I allow him to receive the remaining night designation. He should perform the same formalities as before, mentally resolving and speaking the words aloud.
"I, the bhikṣu [Name], having received the seven-night rule, have [so many] nights remaining. I now receive permission to depart [stated once].
If the circumstances differ (meaning the conditions are not identical), one may again receive the seven-day leave to go."
Section Three: On the Distribution of Deceased Possessions (Thirteen Rules).

First, according to the *Vinaya-saṃgraha*, regarding the six points of harmony for those who have left the household life, the sharing of benefits is counted as one. One who embraces the Way without poverty is called a true Śākyaputra. [This concludes] the *Cīvara-vastu*.
The Buddha’s compassion repeatedly established these prohibitions. Within this compilation, the Patriarch has further elucidated them extensively.

You should contemplate the intent behind their inclusion and refrain from treating them as mere conventional talk. To act upon them whenever circumstances arise is of the utmost urgency and importance (from *Zuochi*).

The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states: "If the deceased is ill and cannot be trusted [to manage his own affairs], one should entrust the door-hook to a monastic administrator (*vaiyāvṛtyakara*) before making offerings to the *śarīra*.
The *Vinayamātṛkā* states: 'First, having taken the deceased away for burial, the monks who accompanied the funeral procession return to the monastery.
They take the deceased's robes and belongings and place them before the assembly of monks; thereafter, the community is convened according to the Dharma.'"
This is how the intent of the Vinaya is seen. As for the ritual procedures according to the Vinaya:

when a bhikṣu within the same boundary dies, the caregiver should immediately inform the administrative officer (karmadāna). The administrative officer shall notify the Upādhyāya and instruct him to strike the bell three times.
Upon hearing this, the assembly shall each remove their outer robes (saṃghāṭī), put on their inner robes (antarvāsaka), and assemble together.
Regarding the niche (kaṅ): there are two meanings to this. First, seeing that the transformations of others are thus, one should admonish oneself to practice with diligence.

Second, it serves to manifest that the assembly of those wearing the *kāṣāya* surpasses ordinary people. After the deceased has been sent away and the cremation performed, they return to the monastery.
If there is no ordination platform (*śīlākṣetra*), one should first dispatch someone to solicit the consent (*chanda*) of the community before instructing the bell to be struck.

Regarding the *gandi*: strike the drum according to the ritual for confession (*kṣamā*), but only fifty-three times. When the great assembly hears it, each person shall adjust their deportment and proceed to the place where the rite is performed.
Once the community of monks has assembled, the administrative officer shall go to the abbot’s quarters to invite the *upādhyāya* to come, making this announcement once again.
The assembly prostrates to the Upādhyāya. (The Upādhyāya says: "You need not bow.
II. The Dharma for Giving Possessions to the Sangha:
(The caregiver, having taken all the deceased’s clothing and belongings and carried them into the midst of the sangha, stands in the center facing upward.)
[The attendant] stands. The administrator calls out.

[The attendant] asks after their health and spreads out the large ritual implements. First, one prostrates three times to the *upādhyāya* (the preceptor). [The *upādhyāya* says: "Prostrate universally at the feet of the monks. The assembly joins their palms in unison.
[After the prostrations,] one asks after their health, kneels long, and joins the palms. [The attendant who cares for the sick says: "I inform you."
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen. The bhikṣu [Name] has passed away at this [or that] residence. All his robes and personal effects should be divided by the Saṃgha present here.
(Recite three times. Then, having prostrated once, rise and stand to one side.)"
3. The Method for Assembling the Sangha and Answering Questions:
After the Preceptor has given the instruction, one performs the preliminary rites (*pūrvakalpa*) and conducts the *karmavācanā* for distributing the robes and belongings of a deceased monk.
4. The Method for Measuring Merit and Awarding Rewards.
The Preceptor said: "Regarding the *karmavācanā*, first one bestows items upon the caregiver; second, one appoints a person by means of a *jñapti-dvitīya-karman*;

and finally, one entrusts the items for distribution. (As for the one performing the ritual, having heard this, he steps out from the assembly toward the upper section; if [the candidate] is exempted, one stops)."

The Master asked the attendant who was caring for the sick person, "When you were attending to the patient at that time, was it because you had been appointed by the monks, or did you take the initiative yourself?

(If he says, "I took the initiative myself," the Master should ask again: "What was your primary intention when you first made up your mind to do so? (If he says, "It was out of a heart of compassion... )
For the sake of benefiting the sick person—and furthermore, because he has always been known to possess the five requisite qualities—the Preceptor addresses the assembly, saying:
"I, [Name], have previously heard that this person attends to the sick in every matter according to the Dharma.
I do not know what the assembly has heard regarding this; if the assembly all says it is indeed as I have described, then [the Preceptor says]: 'Since it is so...'"

There is merit; it is only right that virtue be rewarded. At this time, the three robes, alms bowl, and requisites held by the deceased are to be granted to another through *karmavācanā* (the formal ritual act).

The *vaiyāvṛtyakara* (administrator) shall go to the place where the robes are kept and, weighing the magnitude of the deceased’s meritorious conduct, either grant them all or take only the robes and requisites, along with the bowl, and place them into the hands of one who does not practice the formal rituals (*anupadhivārika*). Having received them, the recipient shall say:

Venerable Saṃgha, listen. Bhikṣu [Name] has passed away. Whatever he possessed—his three robes, alms bowl, sitting mat, needle case, and containers for storing clothing, as they exist at this time, are to be listed—or as it is said:
"whatever various articles and clothing he had"—these should be divided by the present Saṃgha. If the time is right for the Saṃgha, may the Saṃgha grant its consent. The Saṃgha now [or:
taking these various articles and clothing] gives them to the bhikṣu who attended to the sick. Thus is the motion.
Venerable Saṃgha, listen. The bhikṣu [Name] has passed away. All his robes and personal effects should be divided by the present Saṃgha.

The Saṃgha now bestows these robes and effects upon the bhikṣu who attended to the sick. Those elders who consent to the Saṃgha bestowing these robes and effects upon the bhikṣu who attended to the sick, please remain silent.
Whoever does not consent, please speak. The Saṃgha has consented; it bestows [the items] upon [Name].

(Having made this formal announcement, he gives the robes, bowl, and other items to him. The attendant patient then leaves the assembly;
first he should pay respects to the upādhyāya and the great assembly, and only then receive them. This is according to the case of one who possesses all five virtues.)
Regarding the method for rewarding those who tend to the sick of middle or lower status, the amount—whether increased or decreased—should be weighed according to the circumstances at the time.
For example, if one is to give only a single garment, one should announce it by reciting the name of the garment. If the attendant lacks the five virtues, they should not be rewarded;
instead, they may be included among the minor items and the formal procedure performed accordingly. If it is a layperson tending to the sick, a small amount of goods should be given.

and the sick person subsequently dies, this object should be given to that person according to the *Pañcavargika-vinaya* by means of a formal act consisting of one motion and one announcement (*jñapti-dvitīya-karman*).

8. The Method for Indicating the Weight of Objects (Upon hearing this, the person appointed to receive [the items] should immediately leave the assembly, stand to one side within it, and speak as follows).
In the Vinaya, the Buddha said: "If a bhikṣu dies—whether he has many acquaintances or no acquaintances—all his clothing and belongings belong to the Saṃgha.

first, light objects; second, heavy objects. Light objects are those that may be divided; heavy objects are..."
Indivisible items. What are indivisible items? Whatever belongs to a bhikṣu: gardens, fields, fruit trees, separate rooms, and items belonging to those separate rooms;
copper jars, copper basins, axes, chisels, lampstands, rope beds, wooden beds, and raw mattresses.
A bed, a canopy, curtains, a woolen rug, a carriage, a palanquin, a monastery attendant, a water jar, a washbasin, a mendicant’s staff, and a fan.

Furthermore, there are five kinds of manufactured articles: iron articles, wooden articles, ceramic articles, leather articles, and articles made of woven materials, as well as various other heavy objects;

these belong to the Saṃgha of the four quarters and must not be divided. However, if a woolen rug is three cubits long and five cubits wide, with the pile being three finger-breadths thick, it may also be divided. What, then, are the items that may be divided? [The answer is: those belonging to the individual bhikṣu.
The three robes, one alms bowl, sitting mat, needle case, razor, water filter, and the *kuñjara* vessels (translated as "minor items")—these are objects that may be divided;
the *saṃgha* present should divide them. At this time, one should first sort the garments and items by weight, and then weigh them.

Having spoken thus, he immediately sorted the clothing and goods by weight. If they were heavy items, they were to be designated for the general use of the Saṃgha of the four quarters. If they were light items, he examined their quality;
if there was one item for each person, the better ones were distributed in order, beginning with the senior monk (*sthavira*). If there were two items for each person, or more...
Regarding the majority: it is essential that good and evil be weighed against one another to impartially judge the individuals involved. Only absolute fairness constitutes virtue;
one must not yield to personal bias or disregard the law according to one's own likes and dislikes.

(Thus it is said three times. One holds the object and gives it to him. Once he has accepted it, according to the *Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya*, the light object should be received with three utterances by both parties and shared. One person makes the following announcement:)
"Venerable sirs, please bear this in mind: the bhikṣu [Name] has passed away; all his robes and personal effects should belong to us. (Thus it is said three times.

"These belongings of the deceased bhikṣu [Name] should belong to me.

Section Four: The Chapter on the Practice of Concealment (Two Parts). Part One: Granting the *kaṭhina* of Simple Concealment (Fifteen Rules). 1.

With a sense of shame, one confesses the offense before a pure bhikṣu or an official (karmadāna).
Thereupon, that official leads the offender to the *karmavācanā* hall and requests the *karmācārya* to come forth. The official says:
Arrange the ritual implements and perform prostrations; the *karmadāna* performs three prostrations. After the inquiry, [the candidate] kneels long with palms joined.

[The questioner] asks whether he has committed any offenses. [If he has committed any,] having answered truthfully, the administrator calls out: "Stand up! [He] performs three prostrations in gratitude to the *upādhyāya*, rises from his seat, and makes inquiries.

When calculating by the day, one must not yield to personal sentiment. Once the total number of days has been calculated—whether amounting to several thousands, several hundreds, or several tens—one should inquire again in detail.
As for the five grades of minor offenses (*duṣkṛta*), whether they are complete or incomplete, each and every one [must be examined].

6. Examining the phenomena arising therefrom.
The Preceptor said: "As for the *karmavācanā* (formal ritual action), one must first carefully perform repentance for the offenses committed since birth;

One incurs a *duṣkṛta* offense for concealment. On the second day, one should confess this; yet if one does not confess it, there arises another grade of *duṣkṛta* offense for concealment that increases with each passing night.
In this manner, it continues for one night, two nights, up to a hundred thousand nights.

First, one must not confer the full ordination (*upasampadā*) upon others;

Twentieth: One should not commit an offense that is more serious than this. Twenty-first:

Twenty-fourth: One must not accept the leather sandals of a pure bhikṣu.

Twenty-sixth: One must not accept prostrations from a pure bhikṣu.
Twenty-seventh: One must not accept being welcomed or seen off by a pure bhikṣu.
Twenty-eighth: One must not accept the salutations of a pure bhikṣu. Twenty-ninth:

These are the strict regulations established by the Tathāgata. You should respectfully observe each of them one by one. Receive them with faith and practice accordingly.

Section Six: The Chapter on the Completion of the Practice and the Expiation of Offenses (Five Parts).
First, the *karmavācanā* for the expiation of offenses following the completion of the *mānatva* practice alone (Five Rules).

The Buddha said: "When a bhikṣu who has committed a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense has completed the *mānatva* practice, the Saṃgha is permitted to grant him the *karmavācanā* for the expiation of the offense."

A pure assembly of twenty bhikṣus is required; if there are more than twenty, yet one person is missing, the ritual procedure is not accomplished and the offense cannot be cleared (text). This *karmavācanā* for clearing an offense has two types:

first, the *karmavācanā* for clearing an offense without concealment (meaning that when a person who has committed an offense immediately confesses it, and since they lack a mind of concealment, the Vinaya prescribes that they be granted only the *mānatva* penance; once this is completed, the Saṃgha grants the clearing of the offense).
Second, there are four types of *karmavācanā* for the removal of offenses involving concealment (*paryavasthita*), each applied according to the specific transgression.

First, the *karmavācanā* for the removal of offense through the non-destruction of concealment and the non-destruction of *mānatva*. This refers to a person who has committed an offense but did not initially confess it;

having concealed it within their mind, the Vinaya prescribes that they must practice the *parivāsa* (probation) for as many days as the offense was concealed to purify that mind. Once the period of *parivāsa* is completed, they request *mānatva*, and only after practicing *mānatva* is the formal act of removal of the offense (*āpattivyutthāna*) granted. Second, the [removal of offense] through the destruction of concealment... [text fragment ends].
The *mānāpya* (probation) and *āvarhaṇa* (reinstatement) *karmavācanā*: This refers to a bhikṣu who, while practicing *parivāsa*, lacks firmness in the power of faith and commits this offense again.

According to the Vinaya regulations, he is subjected to the *pūrvakalpa* (original penance). Starting again from the beginning, he completes the *pūrvakalpa*. Upon its completion, the *mānāpya* is granted to him. Furthermore, there may be a bhikṣu practicing *mānāpya* whose afflictions are so intense that he cannot subdue them; if he commits this offense again during that interval, the Buddha said: "If there was concealment, grant him the *pracchādana* (concealment) *karmavācanā* once more.

When the *pracchādana* is completed, grant him the *mānāpya* procedure again. If there was no concealment, then grant him the *mānāpya-pūrvakalpa* *karmavācanā* immediately. Once the *pūrvakalpa* is completed, the Saṃgha grants him the *āvarhaṇa* (reinstatement)."

The Master says: Regarding the statement in the text that "repentance brings peace and happiness," there are three meanings. First, it is the cause of peace and happiness.

To regulate and maintain the precepts while recognizing one's faults is what the Vinaya calls being a "wise person. Although the body dwells within the outflows (*āsrava*), the mind remains equal to that of ordinary beings.

As for the "flow": since past habitual tendencies are deep-rooted, they are easily activated by present conditions; yet, one can possess a sense of shame and confess openly, sincerely washing away transgressions.

It is like laundering old clothes: when the grime is exhausted, they remain clean. The ritual procedures of the *vinaya* are likewise: not being distanced from the community, nor mixing improperly with the community, one thus attains peace and happiness.
Second is the peace and happiness of the "flower-retribution," which means that the five categories of offenses have already been purified, and the three increases [of merit]...
It is not yet strong; one does not traverse the evil paths and temporarily receives celestial blessings, thereby attaining peace and happiness. Third is the peace and happiness of karmic retribution:
taking the three untainted trainings as the cause, with *sopadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa* as the fruit. By realizing *nirvāṇa*, one is forever free from all afflictions and does not undergo further existence.
Therefore, it is said that repentance leads to peace and happiness, whereas failing to repent leads to a lack of peace and happiness.

If one commits an offense and conceals it, there will be no way to avoid the two retributions, and one will inevitably go to the three miserable realms; therefore, it is said that "without repentance, there is no peace.

*Dānapati* is a term from the Sanskrit language; here it is translated as "giving" (*dāna*). "Patī" is a word of this region [China], meaning that if a person can practice giving, they will immediately transcend the ocean of suffering of poverty.
"Constant" (*chang*) means remaining unchanging throughout past and present; "abiding" (*zhu*) means not shifting from its location.
It refers to items such as clothing, storage vessels, writing implements, trunks, and baskets.

Regarding the property of the Sangha of the four directions (caturdiśa-saṃgha), it is sometimes referred to as that of the ten directions (daśadik). The "four directions" refers exclusively to ordinary beings (pṛthagjana), whereas the "ten directions" encompasses both the holy (ārya) and the ordinary.
For example, although the substance of the Sangha’s regular food offerings pervades the ten directions, its function is restricted solely to its original location.
There are two kinds of property belonging to the *saṃgha* present before one. First, there is property donated by a donor specifically for the *saṃgha* present at this particular location.

Second, there is light personal property of the five classes of deceased monastics; prior to the performance of the *karmavācanā*, it belongs to the *saṃgha* of the ten directions, but once the formal motion (*jñapti-karman*) has been carried out, it is restricted solely to its original location.
The *Pārivāsika* section of the *Caturvargika-vinaya* speaks of "concealing conduct" (*parivāsa*). The *Vinayaviniscaya-saṃgraha* states: "There are two kinds of concealment:
first, concealment by night; second, concealment by mind. If one conceives a mind of concealment until the dawn light appears, this is called 'one-night concealment'.
The *Mūla-vinaya* speaks of "conduct of wandering about" (*paryuṣitaparivāsa*). The *Vinayaviniscaya-saṃgraha* speaks of "conduct of separate wandering" (*paryuṣitaparivāsa*).
*Mānatva* (摩那埵) is translated in the Han language as "subduing arrogance" (*zhéfú gònggāo*) and also as "lowering one's mind" (*xiàyì*), meaning that one serves the community of monks (*saṃgha*).
In the Qin language, it is called "joy of mind" (*yìxǐ*); it refers to the joy of the mind itself, and it also causes the community of monks to rejoice.
The term for "expiation of offenses" in Sanskrit is *āpattivyutthāna*, which in Chinese is translated as "calling back in" (*huàn rù*) or "extracting the offense" (*bá zuì*); it is thus "expiation.
This means that one becomes eligible to participate together in all ritual proceedings, such as the *poṣadha*, *karmavācanā*, *pravāraṇā*, and the recitation of the precepts.
In the *Mātṛkā-śāstra*, it is called "the arising of pure precepts," meaning that within these precepts one proceeds by maintaining them well, being pure and without transgression.
The *Sudarsana-vinaya* states:
"Sthūla means 'great,' and nigha means 'obstruction'; that is, it obstructs the path to wholesome states. Hereafter...
It leads to rebirth in the evil realms (*durgati*). Its essence is base and defiled; it is named after that which is unwholesome (*akuśala*).
A solitary offense is also termed a *svabhāva-sthūlātyaya*, as it is committed independently.

This refers to, for instance, originally intending to disrupt the *saṃgha* by breaking the *karmavācanā* or turning back the wheel of the Dharma, or intending to steal four *māṣaka* coins or less, and then actually accomplishing what was desired. This is...
It is called "independent" (*pṛthak*).

Regarding "extra robes" (*atireka-cīvara*), it refers to what remains. If one has surplus robe-material that is one chi and six cun in length and eight cun in width, it is termed an "extra robe" and should be formally declared pure (*śuddhi-uddeśa*).
"With-outflow" (*sāsrava*) refers to not cultivating supramundane wholesome dharmas, because one falls into the cycle of birth and death within the three realms.
"Without-outflow" (*anāsrava*) refers to cultivating supramundane wholesome dharmas, because one realizes *nirvāṇa* without remainder.

The three trainings are those of ethical discipline (*śīla*), concentration (*samādhi*), and wisdom (*prajñā*). The three increases are the increase of ethical discipline, the increase of mind, and the increase of wisdom.

Regarding *nirvāṇa*: *ni* means "non-arising" and *vāṇa* means "non-ceasing. Because it is neither arising nor ceasing, it is called *nirvāṇa*. In the language of Qin (Chinese), it is called "unconditioned" (*wuwei*).
It is also translated as "perfect stillness" (*yuanji*) or "nirvana" (*niyuan*). Some translations render it as "peaceful bliss," meaning that [one has already...]

Because one has departed from the thieves of the fetters of affliction (*kleśa-saṃyojana*), there remains residual suffering; that is to say, while the bondage of the seed has been severed, the bondage of the fruit still persists.
*Qu-lü* (pronounced *jǔ lǚ*) refers to a woolen mat; it is also called a woolen cloth, belonging to the class of felt rugs.

Second, there are retributions for past deeds (*vipāka-phala*) and environmental retributions (*adhipati-phala*). Regarding the three miserable realms—hell, hungry ghosts, and animals—the natural environment has never been produced through intentional action (*karma*).
*Āraṇya* is also called *aranya*; the *Mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* translates it as "a place of seclusion and tranquility. Tiantai says: "Not..."

"Seclusion" (*kṣānti*) is so named because it involves performing various tasks; it is called "tranquility" (*śānta*) because it is free from clamor. Alternatively, it may be translated as "non-contention" (*araṇa*), meaning that one's dwelling does not engage in worldly disputes.
This refers to a location five *li* removed from a village.
A *muhūrta*—the Sanskrit name for which is *mahorātra*; in the Abhidharma treatises, it is translated as "a brief moment" (*xūyù*).
There are thirty *muhūrtas* in one day and night; it refers to an extremely short duration of time.
